params.question: In the clinical scenarios described, which condition was revealed by the operating microscope that the auriscope completely failed to detect?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ethmoidal polyps were identified using the rigid nasal endoscope during diagnostic nasal endoscopy, not the operating microscope.

answers.text: Cholesteatoma in the attic of the middle ear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. At 16× magnification the operating microscope revealed a white pearly mass in the attic — cholesteatoma — which the auriscope could not visualise because of wax obstruction and its limited monocular view.

answers.text: Early glottic carcinoma on the vocal cord

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Early glottic carcinoma was detected using the flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscope, which views the vocal cords from above via the nasal route.
Nasal septal perforation was not described in any of the three scenarios. The three conditions were cholesteatoma, ethmoidal polyps, and glottic carcinoma.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three clinical cases: the operating microscope revealed cholesteatoma, the rigid nasal endoscope found ethmoidal polyps, and the flexible laryngoscope detected glottic carcinoma.
Well done. Each of these three instruments addresses a specific anatomical blind spot that basic examination cannot reach.

interactions.label: The Hopkins rod lens system is the optical principle used in the operating micro

params.question: The Hopkins rod lens system is the optical principle used in the operating microscope for oto-microscopy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is false. The Hopkins rod lens system belongs to rigid endoscopes, not the operating microscope. The operating microscope relies on binocular stereoscopic optics with a coaxial light source that keeps the field shadow-free, providing 6–40× magnification with both hands free.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The Hopkins rod lens system is used in rigid endoscopes (nasal and laryngeal), transmitting approximately four times more light than conventional telescopes. The operating microscope uses binocular stereoscopic optics with coaxial illumination and 6–40× magnification.

interactions.label: During diagnostic nasal endoscopy, which pass examines the ostiomeatal complex —

params.question: During diagnostic nasal endoscopy, which pass examines the ostiomeatal complex — the critical drainage corridor for the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses?

answers.text: Pass one along the nasal floor to the nasopharynx

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pass one follows the nasal floor through the inferior meatus to the posterior choana and nasopharynx, inspecting the adenoid pad and Eustachian tube orifices. It does not examine the ostiomeatal complex.

Correct. Pass two angles laterally under the middle turbinate into the middle meatus. Here the ostiomeatal complex — uncinate process, hiatus semilunaris, bulla ethmoidalis, and maxillary sinus ostium — is inspected. Three major sinuses drain through this single corridor.
Pass three examines the sphenoethmoid recess between the middle turbinate and septum, which receives drainage from the sphenoid sinus and posterior ethmoid cells — not the ostiomeatal complex.

There is no separate assessment pass in the standard three-pass DNE technique. Decongestion with xylometazoline and anaesthesia with lignocaine are preparatory steps performed before the scope is introduced.

overallFeedback.feedback: The second pass into the middle meatus is the most important diagnostic pass in DNE. It examines the ostiomeatal complex — the single corridor through which three major sinuses drain.
Exactly right. The middle meatus is the key drainage corridor — disease here affects the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses simultaneously.

interactions.label: On oto-microscopy, a perforation is seen in the pars tensa with an intact surrou

params.question: On oto-microscopy, a perforation is seen in the pars tensa with an intact surrounding rim of membrane and no attic abnormality. Which classification and its management implication is correct?

answers.text: Atticoantral (unsafe) CSOM — urgent surgical referral is needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A central perforation in the pars tensa with an intact rim indicates tubotympanic (safe) disease, not atticoantral. Atticoantral findings involve the pars flaccida or attic region — retraction pockets, keratinous debris, or marginal perforations.

answers.text: Tubotympanic (safe) CSOM — can be managed medically or repaired with elective tympanoplasty

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A central pars tensa perforation with an intact rim is the hallmark of tubotympanic (safe) CSOM. Cholesteatoma is absent, so the disease can be managed medically or repaired with elective tympanoplasty.

The classification as tubotympanic (safe) would be correct, but immediate mastoidectomy is not indicated. Mastoidectomy is reserved for atticoantral (unsafe) disease where cholesteatoma threatens the ossicles, facial nerve canal, or intracranial structures.

answers.text: Atticoantral (unsafe) CSOM — managed with topical antibiotics alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A central perforation with intact rim indicates safe, not unsafe disease. Furthermore, atticoantral disease requires surgical intervention — topical antibiotics alone would be dangerously insufficient.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: a central pars tensa perforation with an intact rim = tubotympanic (safe) CSOM. Attic findings (pars flaccida retraction, keratinous debris, marginal perforation) = atticoantral (unsafe) CSOM requiring surgical referral.
Correct. The central-versus-attic distinction on oto-microscopy drives all subsequent management decisions in chronic suppurative otitis media.

interactions.label: Oto-microscopy in a 28-year-old man with foul-smelling ear discharge reveals whi

params.question: Oto-microscopy in a 28-year-old man with foul-smelling ear discharge reveals white pearly debris in the pars flaccida with scutum erosion. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Aural toilet with topical antibiotic-steroid drops and review in six weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: White pearly debris in the pars flaccida with scutum erosion indicates cholesteatoma (atticoantral/unsafe CSOM). Conservative management risks erosion of the ossicles, facial nerve canal, and potentially life-threatening intracranial complications.

answers.text: Pure tone audiometry and trial of a hearing aid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Audiological assessment may be part of pre-operative workup, but the immediate priority is imaging and surgical referral to address the cholesteatoma before further bony destruction occurs.

answers.text: High-resolution CT of the temporal bone and referral for urgent tympanomastoid surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. White keratinous debris in the pars flaccida with scutum erosion means cholesteatoma until proven otherwise — atticoantral (unsafe) CSOM. HRCT delineates the extent of disease, and urgent tympanomastoid surgery prevents intracranial complications.

Elective tympanoplasty is appropriate for tubotympanic (safe) CSOM with a central perforation. The presence of cholesteatoma makes this atticoantral (unsafe) disease requiring urgent surgical intervention, not elective repair.

overallFeedback.feedback: White keratinous debris in the pars flaccida with scutum erosion = cholesteatoma until proven otherwise. This requires HRCT temporal bone and urgent surgical referral — not conservative management.
Correct. Cholesteatoma demands urgent action — imaging defines the extent of bony erosion and tympanomastoid surgery prevents life-threatening complications.
